title: Restaurant Kitchen Printers: Impact vs. Thermal
description: Kitchen printers face heat, grease, and rush hour. Understand impact vs. thermal so your kitchen tickets never fade or jam.
body:
Your kitchen runs on tickets. When a ticket fades, jams, or prints so quietly the line misses it, food goes out late and mistakes stack up. The single biggest decision you'll make about kitchen printing is impact versus thermal — and the wrong choice shows up fast in a hot, greasy kitchen.

How Impact Printers Work

Impact (dot-matrix) printers strike a ribbon with pins, physically pressing ink onto the paper. Because the print is mechanical rather than heat-based, it doesn't depend on a special coating to stay legible.

What this means in practice:

  • Carbon copies. Impact printers print on multi-ply paper, so one pass gives you two or three identical tickets — one for the line, one for expo, one for the server.
  • Heat resistance. A ticket sitting under a heat lamp won't fade, because the ink isn't heat-activated.
  • Two-color printing. Most impact kitchen printers use a black/red ribbon, letting you flag allergies, rush orders, or modifiers in red.

The trade-offs are real. Impact printers are louder and slower than thermal, and they need ribbon changes. But in a high-heat kitchen where tickets live next to the salamander, that mechanical print is what keeps orders readable.

How Thermal Printers Work

Thermal printers use a heated print head to darken a heat-sensitive coating on the paper. No ribbon, no ink, no moving pins — just heat on paper.

The advantages are immediate:

  • Quiet and fast. Tickets print in well under a second with little noise, which matters during a slammed dinner service.
  • Low maintenance. No ribbons to swap. Your ongoing cost is just the paper roll.
  • Crisp output. Text and modifiers come out sharp and easy to scan at speed.

The limitation is the paper itself. Direct thermal print is heat-sensitive, which means a ticket left under a heat lamp or near a hot pass-through can darken or fade over time. That's the one place thermal struggles in a kitchen — not in printing, but in how the paper holds up after the fact.

Which One Belongs in Your Kitchen

The decision comes down to a few concrete questions about your setup:

  • Do your tickets sit under heat lamps? If the line keeps orders warm under lamps for more than a few minutes, impact paper holds up far better.
  • Do you need carbon copies? If you run separate line, expo, and server copies off a single printer, impact's multi-ply paper is the simplest answer.
  • Is noise a concern? A thermal printer next to the pass won't compete with the ticket machine or the kitchen radio the way an impact unit will.
  • How much are you willing to maintain it? Thermal is nearly maintenance-free; impact needs ribbon swaps and occasional cleaning.

Many kitchens actually run both: an impact printer for hot-side stations where tickets linger, and a thermal printer for the pass or expo where speed and quiet matter more. There's no universal right answer — only the right answer for how your line actually works.

Paper and Ribbon Matter as Much as the Printer

Whichever style you run, the supplies are where kitchens trip up. Impact printers need the correct ribbon and multi-ply paper, and the wrong ribbon means faint, uneven print. Thermal printers need genuine direct thermal paper — heat-sensitive stock that darkens cleanly and won't jam the mechanism. Buying the cheapest roll that technically fits is the fastest way to turn a reliable printer into a recurring headache.

Keep a working spare of whatever your printer uses. A kitchen printer that goes down mid-rush doesn't wait for a restock.

Conclusion

Impact printers win on durability and carbon copies; thermal printers win on speed, quiet, and low maintenance. Match the printer to where the ticket lives — heat lamps and carbon copies favor impact, while a fast, quiet pass favors thermal.
